title: Multiple Personality Parrots
publisher: London South Bank University research portal (Grant, Greenwell & Kolubinski, Applied Animal Behaviour Science 279, 2024)
pageTitle: Owner-rated personality in companion parrots (Aves; Psittaciformes); A four dimension model
quote: A survey of owners of 2200 parrots revealed a four-dimension model of personality: confidence, prosociality, neuroticism and playfulness. There were differences in the levels of these traits between taxonomic groups and variation depending on rearing history and wing clip status. African Grey parrots were lower in confidence than other groups. Hand rearing and wing clipping increased prosociality (perhaps as a substitute for domestication) but with a cost of increased neuroticism.
correctedFact: Parrots have real personalities, and upbringing helps shape them. A survey of owners of 2,200 parrots found four traits: confidence, prosociality, neuroticism and playfulness. Hand-reared and wing-clipped birds came out more sociable but also more neurotic, and African greys scored lower in confidence than the other groups.
note: Personality varies with rearing history and wing clipping, not with the bird's current surroundings, and the study covers parrots generally with one grey-specific finding (lower confidence). No source shows one bird's personality shifting between environments, so 'Multiple Personality' is not supported.

title: Reptile Alarm Clock
publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (Broderick et al. 2007), via PubMed Central
pageTitle: Fidelity and over-wintering of sea turtles
quote: Dive data confirmed that both species conducted much longer deeper dives in winter. ... [green turtle E] January–February 2003, 1.67±1.09 h; range 0.13–5.12 h; n=81 ... [summer] 0.36±0.34 h; range 0.01–1.23 h. Abstract: moving only to deeper waters during the winter months where they demonstrated extremely long resting dives
correctedFact: Green sea turtles can nap underwater for hours. A female green turtle tracked after nesting on Cyprus moved to deeper water in winter and made long resting dives, the longest lasting 5.12 hours on one breath. Her summer foraging dives topped out at about 1.2 hours.
note: The 5 hour figure is real but is a winter maximum from one tracked green turtle (turtle E) in the Mediterranean, not a typical rest. The 10.2 hour record in the abstract belongs to a loggerhead. Body text read via WebFetch (curl hit a reCAPTCHA); a BOEM review citing Hochscheid 2014 gives the same green turtle maximum as 307.0 minutes. 'Dive deep' and 'most efficient swimmers' remain unsupported.

title: Singing Spiders
note: Five searches on Parasteatoda (Achaearanea) tepidariorum courtship vibration, web plucking, stridulation and Theridiidae signaling found only relatives (black widow, Steatoda grossa, hobo spider Tegenaria agrestis, Argiope); Vibert et al. 2014 even found black widow and hobo spider courtship lacks complex 'songs'. Nothing on the common house spider itself.

title: Octopus Ink Defense
pageTitle: Cephalopod Ink: Production, Chemistry, Functions and Applications
quote: However, ink from octopus ink was found to be attractive to moray eels, evoking searching and attack behaviors, much as did food-related chemicals [117]. To date, there are no reports of experimental tests of cephalopod ink as an inactivator or disruptor of the chemical senses.
correctedFact: Octopus ink is a smoke screen, not a nose plug. The dark cloud lets an octopus hide or jet away. Scientists have proposed that ink scrambles a predator's sense of smell, but nobody has tested it, and in one study octopus ink actually attracted moray eels and set off searching and attacks.
note: The smell-impairing idea is untested per the review, and the one chemical test with a predator (Grüninger 1997, moray eels and Octopus bimaculoides) found octopus ink attractive, the opposite effect. 'Smoke-screens behind which inking cephalopods can hide or jet escape' is from the same page.

title: Feline Mustache
quote: There are usually no whiskers but if whiskers are present they are short and sparse.
correctedFact: Sphynx cats look bald but are not always totally hairless, often keeping short hair on the nose, ears and tail. Whiskers are the real surprise: most Sphynx have none at all, and any that do grow are short and sparse. No mustache here, just a sweet-tempered, lively cat with delicate skin.
note: Same CFA page as the first pass (cached as F_sphynx_cfa.txt) holds the whisker line plus 'not always totally hairless', 'Some short hair is usually present on the nose, ears and tail', 'delicate' skin and 'sweet-tempered, lively'. CFA's whisker article (G_catwhisker_cfa.txt) adds Sphynx whiskers 'are often stubbly'. 'Just as sensitive as ours' stays unsupported.

title: Invisible Wings
note: No booby-specific study on underwater vision found. Closest: Machovsky-Capuska et al. 2012, Proc R Soc B (PMC3441088), shows Australasian gannets' eyes accommodate 'immediately upon submergence of the head' and overcome the loss of over 45 D of corneal power; gannets are booby relatives but the paper never mentions boobies. Card's 'up to 30 feet' also conflicts with DLNR's 13 to 26 feet.

title: Tube-Eyed Head Rotators
publisher: University of Illinois College of Veterinary Medicine (Wildlife Medical Clinic blog)
pageTitle: Owl Oddities - Veterinary Medicine at Illinois
quote: Owls' eyes are not circular like humans! The main reason why owls evolved to be able to rotate their head so much is because their eyes do not move. An owl's eyes are tube or cylinder shaped, and they do not move in their sockets as normal human and mammal eyes do. ... One of the proposed reasons for this is because of owls' phenomenal night vision. ... owls can rotate their heads a whopping 270 degrees
correctedFact: Owls don't have round eyeballs like ours. Their eyes are tube shaped and sit fixed in their skull sockets, so they can't move them at all. Instead, owls swivel their heads a whopping 270 degrees, not quite the full circle people imagine. Built-in swivel mode activated!
note: Supported as written; correctedFact is offered only to remove the spaced-hyphen dash in the card. Page is written by a vet student (Class of 2026) on the vet school's clinic blog, consistent with the Owl Research Institute's sclerotic ring line.

title: Faster Than a Fighter Pilot
newTitle: More G's Than a Fighter Jet
publisher: Smithsonian Magazine (Smart News, Maris Fessenden, Jan 6, 2016)
pageTitle: Tiny Chameleon's Tongue Can Beat the Fastest Sports Car
quote: The unfurling of Rhampholeon spinosus's elastic, sticky tongue involves an acceleration of the specialized muscle of up to 264 times the force of gravity ... In comparison, he adds, NASA's space shuttle accelerates to 3 g to propel itself into orbit—jet fighters flying F-16s only reach 7g when they pull out of a dive.
correctedFact: A tiny chameleon, Rhampholeon spinosus, launches its sticky tongue with an acceleration of up to 264 times the force of gravity. For comparison, the space shuttle hit 3 g on its way to orbit, and F-16 fighter jets reach only 7 g when pulling out of a dive.
note: The source compares with what an F-16 reaches in a dive pull-out, not with what a pilot can withstand, and the 264 g peak is for one small species. 'Snap back with its prey in a fraction of a second' is still unsupported. Page read via WebFetch (curl hit a Cloudflare challenge).
